strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and model architectures with consistent improvements
Well-motivated adaptation of fill-in-the-middle from code reasoning to mathematical problem-solving with practical benefits
Thoughtful ablation studies disentangling distillation effects, iterative expansion, and model scale impacts
Computational efficiency compared to MCTS-based approaches, with small models (1.5B) achieving competitive results
Practical contributions through release of NuminaMath-FIM dataset and MathFimer-7B model
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-structured methodology
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty—straightforward application of existing FIM techniques with minimal methodological innovation
Inconsistent and minimal improvements on competition-level mathematics (Math Odyssey, OlympiadBench-EN), with some negative results, suggesting limited scalability to harder reasoning tasks
Critical hyperparameter η = 0.8 for similarity filtering appears ad-hoc with no ablation study, justification, or sensitivity analysis
Contradictory evidence on correctness preservation: Figure 4 shows G+M expanded steps with lower PRM scores despite claims of maintaining correctness
Data confound in multi-iteration experiments—token count increases (+232%) make it unclear whether improvements come from method or data augmentation alone
Incomplete failure mode analysis—no systematic investigation of when/why method fails, particularly on harder problems
Limited baseline comparisons—Table 5 uses unfair cross-paper comparisons; prompt-based baseline uses only one model
Rule-based step decomposition may not be optimal; no analysis of decomposition quality impact on downstream performance
Missing computational overhead analysis—no inference time, memory, or training cost comparisons vs. baseline approaches
Generalization concerns—only tested on mathematical reasoning; claims about scalability cannot be assessed in other domains
Insufficient justification for why FIM should work for math vs. code—different reasoning structures not addressed
LLM-as-judge evaluation without human evaluation or robustness guarantees

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple base models (8B/70B), training datasets (5 total), and benchmarks (4 total)
Extensive ablation studies analyzing distillation effects, iteration effects, and model scale sensitivity
Honest discussion of limitations and methodological constraints in Appendix A
Practical efficiency by achieving step expansion with relatively modest models (1.5B-7B) rather than massive external models
Clear motivation for adapting FIM from code completion to mathematical reasoning with intuitive framing
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward application of existing FIM technique to math step expansion with minimal algorithmic contribution
Inconsistent and modest improvements across settings (many <1%, some negative: e.g., +0.29% on MetaMathQA, -0.36% on NuminaMath-CoT with Qwen 7B; improvements diminish on stronger models)

Problematic evaluation methodology: non-standard sampling at T=0.7 with 16 samples (vs. greedy T=0), reliance on unspecified LLM-as-judge, and absence of statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Confounding factors inadequately controlled: distillation alone provides >10% gains (Table 2) that dwarf FIM's marginal contribution; data quality heavily impacts results (Table 8) limiting generalization

Incomplete comparison with related work: no direct head-to-head comparison with MCTS, rejection sampling, or RL methods; Table 5 uses different base models/settings making fair comparison impossible; prompt baseline is simplistic
Arbitrary design choices lack justification: similarity threshold η=0.8 has no ablation; random step sampling creates selection bias; why T=0.7 for evaluation not discussed
Missing critical analyses: no error analysis, conditional effectiveness analysis, qualitative step quality evaluation, computational cost comparison, or failure case discussion
High baseline quality in PRM scores (87-94%, Figure 4) limits room for improvement; iterative expansion sustainability and error accumulation through iterations not addressed
Improvements scale poorly to stronger models (70B/72B show diminishing returns), limiting practical utility for state-of-the-art systems
Overclaimed contributions and language (e.g., 'groundbreaking,' 'practical scalable solution') overstating modest and inconsistent results

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 base model sizes, 5 source datasets, and 4 evaluation benchmarks with consistent improvements
Practical and efficient approach that doesn't require external powerful models or MCTS-style search, achieving comparable results with small models (1.5B parameters)
Thorough ablation studies examining distillation effects, iteration benefits, model scale impacts, and comparison with alternative methods
Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of existing step expansion approaches; clear preservation of solution validity
Strong empirical results with iterative improvements up to 15.54% across multiple benchmarks and architectures
Released resources (NuminaMath-FIM dataset and MathFimer models) provide practical value to the community
Clear presentation with informative figures and well-structured methodology
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: straightforward adaptation of existing FIM task to mathematical domain; core technical contribution is incremental
Critical design choice (similarity threshold η=0.8) appears arbitrary with no ablation study or sensitivity analysis provided
Insufficient error analysis and understanding of error propagation, particularly concerning for iterative expansion where mistakes could compound
Evaluation methodology concerns: LLM-as-judge specification incomplete; no discussion of potential biases; lacks exact match evaluation where applicable
Strong dependency on high-quality initial data demonstrated in Appendix E (significant performance drops with lower-quality sources), limiting applicability
Missing computational cost analysis despite claims of efficiency; no discussion of wall-clock time, memory requirements, or inference costs for large-scale expansion
Step decomposition is rule-based and somewhat ad-hoc; no analysis of how decomposition quality affects downstream performance
Incomplete comparisons with related work: different base models in Table 5 limit direct comparison; limited direct evaluation against MCTS and other expansion methods
Statistical rigor insufficient: no significance tests, inconsistent error bars, unclear which improvements are statistically meaningful given sampling-based evaluation
Generalization concerns not thoroughly investigated: only mathematical reasoning evaluated despite originating from code reasoning paradigm

strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing practical limitations of existing step expansion methods
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 base models, 5 datasets, and 4 evaluation benchmarks with consistent improvements (+0.3% to +8.86%)
Thorough ablation studies (iteration effects, model scale, distillation decomposition) that provide good insights
Rigorous quality assessment using PRM with 94% agreement with human evaluation; ~90% of generated steps achieve high quality
Practical efficiency demonstrated with small models (1.5B parameters) effectively performing step expansion
Strong empirical results showing generalization across model architectures and scales
Detailed reproducibility information and promise to release models and datasets
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty - primarily adapts existing FIM from code completion to math without fundamental innovation
Critical hyperparameter (similarity threshold η=0.8) lacks justification, sensitivity analysis, or guidance for dataset selection
Strong dependency on high-quality training data (NuminaMath-CoT); performance degrades significantly on lower-quality data, severely limiting applicability
Incomplete error analysis - limited discussion of failure modes, and performance regressions on some benchmarks without thorough investigation
Weak comparisons with alternatives - Table 4 uses only one baseline model, Table 5 uses different base models/datasets, and no comparison with other step-expansion methods in main paper
Computational costs not documented - no training time, inference time, or quantitative efficiency comparison with alternatives despite efficiency claims
Significant applicability limitations explicitly identified: incompatible with refined reasoning (R1-style), non-linear reasoning structures, and code reasoning
Diminishing returns on iteration - sublinear improvements with each iteration and plateau effects on several benchmarks by iteration 3
Inconsistent PRM filtering results (Table 12) suggest expansion introduces noise difficult to filter, undermining quality narrative
Statistical significance unclear - many improvements lack error bars and some gains <1% without significance testing
Overstated generalization claims - OOD evaluation shows mixed results (+16% on BBH but minimal gains elsewhere) and limited ReasoningFimer experiments
Insufficient justification for design decisions: why PSM ordering, why 3 random samples, sensitivity to step decomposition quality unexplored
Design choices appear somewhat arbitrary (e.g., 0.8 similarity threshold, rule-based decomposition vs. learned segmentation)
Baseline comparisons primarily against original data without comparisons to other data augmentation strategies

strengths: Clear problem motivation and well-structured paper with comprehensive experimental coverage across multiple base models and benchmarks
Extensive ablation studies including model effects disentanglement, iteration analysis, and domain applicability evaluation
Practical approach that doesn't require stronger external models, with promise of releasing NuminaMath-FIM dataset and MathFimer-7B
Transparent acknowledgment of limitations including failure modes for non-linear reasoning and already-refined data
Demonstrates that step expansion task doesn't require very large models (Table 3b)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—straightforward application of existing FIM technique from code to math without fundamental methodological advances

Inconsistent and often marginal improvements, particularly on competition-level math (MATH: +0.46-3.52%, with some negative results like -0.78%). Claim of 'consistent improvements' contradicted by regressions in multiple configurations

Critical evaluation concerns: (1) LLM-as-a-judge reliability for math; (2) PRM scores show 87-94% of original steps already high-quality, questioning added value; (3) Limited human evaluation (100 examples, 2 annotators); (4) No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals provided

Severe applicability limitations explicitly acknowledged but inadequately addressed: fails on non-linear/tree-structured reasoning, offers limited benefits for already-refined data, risks error propagation during iteration

Single-pass expansion in main experiments due to computational constraints makes practical utility unclear. Iterative expansion (Table 3) requires 232-350% more tokens for only modest additional gains
High sensitivity to training data quality (Appendix H): MetaMathQA-trained FIM produces much weaker results than NuminaMath-CoT-trained, limiting generalizability

Weak baseline comparisons: prompt-based baseline uses general 3B model instead of strong math models (Table 4); other methods compared with different models/settings (Table 5); missing direct comparison with MCTS-based approaches
Arbitrary design choices lacking justification: similarity threshold η=0.8 (no sensitivity analysis), random step selection rationale unexplored, three sampling rounds unexplained
Marginal gains on harder benchmarks contradict claims of broad applicability—why do improvements on Olympiad-level math (Odyssey: -0.51 to +1.54%) dwarf those on easy benchmarks?

Missing key analyses: qualitative characterization of inserted steps (examples in Appendix L show some redundancy), computational cost comparison to alternatives, proportion of truly novel vs. paraphrased steps

strengths: Clear problem motivation: well-articulated critique of existing step expansion methods and compelling research question about efficient expansion while preserving solution validity
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: extensive experiments across 4 base models, 5 datasets, and 4 benchmarks with consistent improvements (+7.43% GSM8K, +8.86% MATH)
Thorough ablation studies: disentangles FIM effects from distillation, analyzes iterative expansion, model scale sensitivity, and domain applicability
Practical value and reproducibility: releases NuminaMath-FIM dataset and MathFimer-7B model, works with modest model sizes (1.5B), detailed hyperparameters provided
Good presentation and examples: clear motivation, well-organized paper, concrete examples in appendices illustrate step expansion effectively
Complementarity with other methods: demonstrates orthogonality with RL/DPO approaches, expanded data serves as better starting point for subsequent optimization
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: straightforward application of existing FIM technique from code to math domain without significant methodological innovation
Quality control concerns: ad-hoc similarity threshold (η=0.8) lacks ablation study, 10% of steps potentially problematic despite high PRM scores, only 100 samples for human-PRM agreement verification
Incomplete failure case analysis: several performance regressions unexplained, missing guidance on when NOT to use method, no characterization of problem types that benefit vs. suffer from expansion

Weak comparative analysis: comparisons with DPO/PPO/RFT use different base models/datasets, no head-to-head comparison with other step expansion methods, missing control experiment with longer sequences/more data

Token/data analysis insufficient: dramatic token increases (232% for 3 iterations) raise verbosity concerns, counterintuitive: PRM scores sometimes decrease after expansion yet downstream performance improves
Overstated domain generalization claims: OOD results are modest and mixed, ReasoningFimer results particularly weak with limited analysis
Computational cost not thoroughly discussed: claimed efficiency over MCTS but no detailed comparisons, cost of expanding large datasets not quantified, training requires non-standard Ascend hardware
Reproducibility concerns: Ascend H910B-64G hardware not widely available, sequence similarity computation not fully specified, code/data release not explicitly confirmed
